title: JEE Main Tie-Breaking Rules: What Actually Decides Your Rank on a Tie
description: Same percentile as someone else isn't the end of the story. Here's the full eight-step order NTA uses to break a tie, with a worked example.
author: Studyloaf Team

content.body: Two candidates can land on the exact same NTA percentile in JEE Main. When that happens, NTA doesn't just assign them the same rank and move on. There's a specific order of tie-breaking criteria applied before falling back to a shared rank. Knowing the order matters, because it changes how you might think about where to spend your last few weeks of prep if you're chasing every possible edge.

content.heading: The actual order
content.body: For Paper 1 (B.Tech/B.E.), when candidates are tied on percentile, NTA breaks the tie in this sequence:

rows: Incorrect to correct answers, all subjects

content.heading: Where this order comes from
content.body: The order above is NTA's tie-breaking policy as published in the JEE Main information bulletin since the 2025 cycle. It is based entirely on subject scores and accuracy. Up to 2024 the list also used age and application number as final tie-breakers, so advice saying "the younger candidate wins ties" describes the pre-2025 rules and no longer applies.

content.heading: A worked example
content.body: Say two candidates, A and B, land on the exact same overall percentile. A scored higher in Physics but lower in Math than B. B scored higher in Math. Since Mathematics is checked first, B wins the tie regardless of how Physics or Chemistry compare. The process never even reaches those subjects, because the tie was already resolved at step 1.

content.heading: What this actually means for how you prepare
content.body: This isn't a reason to suddenly neglect Physics or Chemistry. The tie-break only matters if you're already percentile-tied with someone else, a fairly narrow situation. But it is a genuine, if small, argument for not leaving Mathematics as your weakest of the three if you have any flexibility in how you allocate remaining practice time, since it's the first subject checked. The accuracy-ratio criteria (steps 4 to 7) are also a quiet reminder that blind guessing on questions you have zero basis for can hurt you in a way that shows up specifically in a tie scenario, even if the overall expected-value math on a single question still favors an educated guess.

If you want to see how your accuracy per subject is actually trending across practice sessions (since that's what steps 4 to 7 are really about), Studyloaf's free timer lets you tag sessions by subject, no account needed, so you can check whether your negative-to-positive ratio in Math specifically is where you'd want it before exam day.
